The Qarmatians: A Pioneering Experiment in Socialism
passage-en-00454

Ibn Rizam claimed that Hamdan Qarmat gathered men and women together on a particular night, when they would mingle. What drove this accusation was his fierce loyalty to the Ismaili movement, from which the Qarmatians had broken away. He tarred them with the vilest accusations in order to discredit them and diminish their standing.
The Qarmatians: A Pioneering Experiment in Socialism
passage-en-00455

Professor Ulyan rejects these accusations. The Qarmatians were careful to observe and preserve the laws of inheritance. Women held a respected place in Qarmatian society, and the marriage bond was known to be strong. None of this is consistent with the idea of sexual licence.
The Qarmatians: A Pioneering Experiment in Socialism
passage-en-00456

Professor Abd al-Jalil Hasan makes a different argument. Mazdakism and the Khurramite movement were both revolutionary social movements. They declared war on the class system and sought justice and equality. Their revolutionary teachings included a rejection of the outdated social arrangements that kept people locked into their social classes, and an effort to relax excessively strict marriage laws for the benefit of oppressed people. Mazdak, for instance, taught that a man could give up one of his wives so that another man who had fallen into poverty could marry her. This, we believe, was a humane principle adopted by the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) when he brought the Emigrants from Mecca and the Helpers of Medina together in a bond of brotherhood. A man from among the Helpers would divorce one of his wives so that an Emigrant could marry her. Abd al-Jalil also refutes the claim that the Khurramites — whose name, in the interpretation of the movement's enemies, meant a doctrine of pleasure — advocated sexual licence. He points to the contradictions in the accounts of their beliefs. While al-Baghdadi, for instance, claims that the Khurramites practised the sharing of sexual partners, elsewhere he says that “they built mosques for Muslims and taught their children the Quran”.
The Qarmatians: A Pioneering Experiment in Socialism
passage-en-00457

In short, the accusations levelled at the Qarmatians — that they believed in divine indwelling and the passage of souls from one body to another, and advocated licence and forbidden acts — are at odds with the nature of the movement and its honourable historical record.
The Qarmatians: A Pioneering Experiment in Socialism
passage-en-00458

What is beyond doubt, however, is that the Qarmatian experiment drew on a legacy of enlightened ideas in both Eastern and Western systems and theories. It adapted those ideas to the needs of the age without coming into conflict with the teachings of Islam. We believe that the Qarmatians drew on the scientific revival and intellectual awakening of the period in spreading their message and organising their society. The advances in astronomy made by the Sabians of Harran, for instance, were reflected in the philosophy behind their underground movement, as we noted earlier. They also drew on the ideas Plato put forward in his Republic in establishing their political and social institutions. Plato's ideas influenced later schools of thought in East and West alike and found an echo in Islamic philosophy. Sabine goes so far as to say that Plato's Republic was a book for every age, from which later generations drew inspiration for the most diverse schools of thought.
The Qarmatians: A Pioneering Experiment in Socialism
passage-en-00459

In the Republic, Plato tried to establish the essential principles, or lay down the best possible plan for an ideal republic, or “virtuous city”. It would be free of all the evils and wrongs that had plagued every society known to him. Virtue would flourish, justice would prevail and its inhabitants would live in harmony. But Plato carried his idealism too far, and his Republic offered a vision of a perfect society that was difficult to realise. Although he abandoned many of his earlier views when he came to write his Laws, recognising that he had gone too far, Muslim philosophers followed in his footsteps and drew heavily on his ideas. The Brethren of Purity, who emerged in the middle of the fourth century AH, after the foundation of the Qarmatian state, drew inspiration from Plato's Republic in writing many of their essays. But even before the Qarmatian movement appeared, a Muslim philosopher like al-Farabi had written his Views of the People of the Virtuous City, modelled on Plato's Republic. There is no doubt that al-Farabi brought together the ideas of Plato, the philosophy of Aristotle and the principles of Islam. He offered a new vision of an ideal society that was likewise difficult to realise. The Qarmatians, however, were the first to put a distinctively Islamic version of such a vision into practice. We can see this by looking at the points of similarity and agreement between Plato's ideal society and the Qarmatian experiment.
The Qarmatians: A Pioneering Experiment in Socialism
passage-en-00460

Plato based his philosophy on his understanding of the human soul. He believed that it contained three forces: reason, spirit and desire. Accordingly, he divided the work of his republic among three groups: the rulers, the guardians and the producers. All three groups were to be educated and prepared for their roles from childhood. The rulers received a special education to develop wisdom and sound judgement, becoming philosophers. The guardians were taught courage and the willingness to face danger. The producers were brought up to value work, self-restraint and moderation. All three groups were bound together by brotherhood, equality and cooperation, with the happiness of everyone as their sole aim. The only distinction between the groups lay in the work they did. Plato believed that justice could not be achieved so long as private ownership existed. He therefore called for its abolition, regarding it as a grave evil. He also advocated the communal sharing of partners among the guardians, although he later abandoned this idea in his Laws, praised family life and stressed the importance of strengthening family bonds.
The Qarmatians: A Pioneering Experiment in Socialism
passage-en-00461

How far was this philosophy reflected in the Qarmatian experiment? The sources describe an enlightened and discerning group in whose hands political power rested. At its head was a just ruler, no despot, who sought guidance from a council known as the aqdaniyya — those with the authority to make and undo binding decisions. This principle of consultation is the backbone of political democracy in Islam. The members of the council stood on equal terms with their ruler, who was himself one of them, primus inter pares — first among equals. He enjoyed no special privilege over them and ruled with justice and fairness, guided by the advice of his peers. He was known as the master, and they as the “counsellors” (al-ashira). All of them belonged to the movement and had been initiated into the secrets of knowledge and wisdom. Is this form of government not strikingly similar to the rule of philosophers envisaged by Plato? These were people who had grasped the universal meaning of justice, beauty and the highest good. No single philosopher held power alone; the philosophers governed through collective consultation.
The Qarmatians: A Pioneering Experiment in Socialism
passage-en-00462

In Qarmatian society, responsibility for defence fell to a distinct body of warriors who received a purely military upbringing from childhood, in accordance with an established system of education. They were brought together in special houses and trained in horsemanship and the use of arms. Al-Maqrizi tells us that the fighting force of al-Ahsa numbered twenty thousand soldiers, ready for sacrifice and renowned for their courage in battle. It seems clear, then, that the Qarmatians were influenced in this respect by Plato's ideas about the guardians. They were given physical training from childhood and, from the age of twelve, went on to military training, devoting themselves entirely to defence.
The Qarmatians: A Pioneering Experiment in Socialism
passage-en-00463

The producers of Qarmatian society, meanwhile, carried out their role remarkably well. Nasir Khusraw tells us that thirty thousand people in al-Ahsa worked on farms and in gardens. Workers and artisans were organised into groups according to their trades, and even women and children had particular tasks to perform, as al-Nuwayri also notes.
The Qarmatians: A Pioneering Experiment in Socialism
passage-en-00464

The Qarmatians also offered assistance to any craftsman who came to settle in their state, providing homes for such people at the community's expense. There is thus a striking resemblance between the way working people were organised in Qarmatian society and Plato's idea of a distinct group of producers whose lives were founded on dedication, self-restraint, cooperation and moderation.
The Qarmatians: A Pioneering Experiment in Socialism
passage-en-00465

The high standing enjoyed by women in Qarmatian society and their equality with men in sharing responsibilities and burdens also find a parallel in Plato's commitment to equality between the sexes. In his system of education, he made no distinction between boys and girls. He recognised the need to put the full abilities of every member of society to use in the service of the state.
The Qarmatians: A Pioneering Experiment in Socialism
passage-en-00466

We can therefore say that the Qarmatians drew heavily on Plato's ideas when they established their experiment in socialism in Iraq and Bahrain. But they adapted those ideas to the realities of their society and gave them a distinctive character, founded above all on the Islamic principle of justice.

This study caught the attention of scholars and of readers interested in Islamic thought. The magazine Rose al-Yusuf opened its pages to their comments, most of which were either critical or supportive of the approach I had taken. It seems useful to reproduce the criticisms and my replies as they appeared at the time. For the favourable responses, I will quote selected passages from the articles in question.
1 — Critical Views
passage-en-00470
The first to speak out against the study was Ahmad Musa Salim, who wrote an article entitled:
The Secret Movements in Islamic History Were a Counter-Revolution
passage-en-00471

Here is what he wrote:
The Secret Movements in Islamic History Were a Counter-Revolution
passage-en-00473

In the last issue of Rose al-Yusuf, I read an article by Dr Mahmoud Ismail entitled “Secret Political Movements in Islam”. My first reaction was amazement at the sheer wealth of information brimming over in the good doctor's article. In all its variety, it reminded me of red, silver and yellow ornamental fish swimming around a glass bowl, trying to find their way out. But from the point of view of a believing Muslim society fighting for its future on our Arab soil, these ideas and pieces of information are both false and dangerous. I hoped, therefore, to take up some of the work of the Muslims who had confronted and corrected such ideas before me. I want to apply the test of scholarly honesty to our understanding of the nature of Islam and the history of the Arab nation that fought for it. And I would like to point out to the author, if he is willing to listen, that the ideas he repeats from others, imagining them to be scientific and objective, are nothing but inventions that feed off Islam and attack it. They die the moment they come into contact with the living reality they seek to penetrate.
The Secret Movements in Islamic History Were a Counter-Revolution
passage-en-00474

The author's lengthy article boils down to this: the secret political movements that eventually brought down Arab rule in the Arab homeland — among them the Qarmatians, the Ismailis and the Kharijites — were, in his view, engaged in a legitimate struggle against what he calls the hereditary monarchy of the Umayyads and the Abbasids' Persian-style religious monarchy. He even sees them as early forms of the progressive Islamic left.
The Secret Movements in Islamic History Were a Counter-Revolution
passage-en-00475

The article has a purpose, of course. After a long series of barbs and claims hostile to the Arabs, it aims to persuade modern Muslims that Islam is a revolution that depends on organised underground activity — the very opposite of its true nature. Through such activity, we are supposed to believe, the likes of the Qarmatians and the Ismaili followers of hidden religious teachings proved that Muhammad's call to the Quran and Islam was a revolution of the left.
The Secret Movements in Islamic History Were a Counter-Revolution
passage-en-00476

Before going any further, I would do well to remind the author of a simple truth. An impartial study of the long story of religion — the true religion revealed by God — from the life of Abraham to that of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon them both, shows that the finest moments in the struggle of the prophets were those when they spoke out openly, with a clear and resounding call to God. They stood without fear, without disguises and without secret activity before kings who claimed divine powers and arrogant tyrants. This openness, backed by proof and strength, is part of the very nature of religion: its way of explaining life and its purpose of transforming the human soul through faith.
The Secret Movements in Islamic History Were a Counter-Revolution
passage-en-00477
To brush aside this truth, clear as the sun, the author assembles a whole range of old and new ideas and beliefs hostile to the Arabs. I need only point to a few of them here:
The Secret Movements in Islamic History Were a Counter-Revolution
passage-en-00478
He tries to present a modern anti-Arab interpretation of Islam based on the materialist view of history. To do so, he summarises Bandali Jawzi's book, The History of Intellectual Movements in Islam.
The Secret Movements in Islamic History Were a Counter-Revolution
passage-en-00479

Jawzi sees Muhammad's call as an example of a revolution led by a national leader who felt the pain of slaves and the poor and rallied them against the wealthy ruling class of Mecca. As you can see, this is a naive and sterile attempt to impose materialist thinking on Islam. There is not a trace of scientific, impartial study of the history of religion or the history of the Arabs. As far as we know, both stretch back thousands of years.
The Secret Movements in Islamic History Were a Counter-Revolution
passage-en-00480

Following in Jawzi's footsteps, the author tries to divide Muslims into a left and a right. Yet for those who believe in Islam, it is neither right nor left. It is “certain knowledge”. Its principles for shaping and developing the individual and society go beyond the left's theories of progress, just as they reject the right's means of oppression. Indeed, if we must judge by the standards of materialist thinking, true Islam is entirely on the left compared with the backward, godless right represented by these secret Qarmatian and Ismaili movements. The author celebrates them, even though they were counter-revolutions directed against Islam.
The Secret Movements in Islamic History Were a Counter-Revolution
passage-en-00481

The author admits that the Qarmatians and others drew on ideas that had no Islamic roots: Greek thought, Jewish traditions concerned with hidden spiritual knowledge, and pagan beliefs from the East. Yet he tries to defend them with prejudiced and academically dishonest claims. With the brazen hostility of an anti-Arab partisan, he accuses the community of the Prophet's city and the first home of Islam of having built its religious mission on the legacy of other civilisations. He claims that the Islamic empire owed its culture and civilisation — as Zionist Orientalist scholarship claims — to the Library of Alexandria, Christian monasteries, Jewish synagogues and Zoroastrian fire temples.
The Secret Movements in Islamic History Were a Counter-Revolution
passage-en-00482
Can this be taken seriously?
The Secret Movements in Islamic History Were a Counter-Revolution
passage-en-00483

He tries to make the word “Qarmatians” the recurring refrain in his anti-Arab song. Through it, he offers an idea alien to religion and false to history: that the Qarmatians were Muslim revolutionaries fighting for freedom within “communes”, which he considers the ideal form of organised revolutionary action in Islam. Yet it is well known that the Qarmatian movement was one of the secret movements that sought to establish a settler presence in the Arab homeland, aiming to conquer it from within through ideas and beliefs and pave the way for military conquest from outside.
The Secret Movements in Islamic History Were a Counter-Revolution
passage-en-00484

According to Father Anastas al-Karmali, in his explanation of the name derived from their leader, Hamdan ibn Qarmat, the Qarmatians' name comes from the Aramaic word qarmatuna, meaning “deceiver” or “wicked man”. Was the leftist Hamdan ibn Qarmat, who emerged from the secret cellars of the counter-revolution against Islam in the town of Salamiyya, a desecrator or a progressive?
The Secret Movements in Islamic History Were a Counter-Revolution
passage-en-00485

Throughout their bloody underground history, the Qarmatians were paid agents of foreign conquest and deceivers who led a counter-revolution against Islam. In pursuit of their plans for settler conquest, they set about slaughtering Muslims, looting property, permitting immoral acts, treating women as common property, attempting to destroy the Kaaba and promoting secret leaders whom they claimed were infallible and divine. Could anyone addressing Muslims honestly call this progressive action?
The Secret Movements in Islamic History Were a Counter-Revolution
passage-en-00486

In closing, my hope is not so much to change Dr Mahmoud Ismail's ideas as to persuade him to reconsider the worth of the evidence and information he relies on. I would also like him to recognise that modern progressive Arab action after the Egyptian revolution of 1952 and the resistance struggle on which it draws — both of them resting on greater clarity, understanding and commitment to the nature of faith and the truth of Islam — are founded on openness, clarity, honesty in matters of belief and revolutionary purity, not on secret activity or covert infiltration.
The Secret Movements in Islamic History Were a Counter-Revolution
passage-en-00487

Above all, I hope everyone who read that article will recognise the dangers it contains. In our age, we badly need to renew our culture from its original sources, on the basis of a sound understanding of Islam and Arab history. Only then will intellectuals break their habit of always making their ideas dance to the tunes of the two superpowers: the right or the left.
The Secret Movements in Islamic History Were a Counter-Revolution

Criticising an Approach Without Having One

Here is the text:
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00491
At first, I had no wish to respond to Ahmad Musa Salim. I thought entering into a dispute of this kind would be a rather foolish exercise, leading to nothing but a pointless exchange of insults.
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00492

In the end, however, I became convinced that a reply was necessary. It was time to expose the false claims of those who boast of their ability to “confront and correct ideas in the light of scholarly honesty”, and those who wrongly appoint themselves defenders of Islam — as though Islam needed their services! Wielding intimidation as a weapon, they do a disservice to the tolerance of Islam and go against its sound approach to debate through “example and kindly advice”.
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00493
It is in this very spirit of true Islam that I will engage with Mr Salim.
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00494

The first thing to point out is that he has failed to grasp what the author means by right and left. He confuses Islam as a noble faith with the political system of the Islamic world under the Umayyads and Abbasids. From there, he slips into the mistaken belief that criticism of the caliphate amounts to an attack on Islam, forgetting that the caliphs are human beings who can be right or wrong. Some were just and others unjust. History subjects all of them to criticism as political rulers, not as infallible religious leaders. As Dr Taha Hussein puts it, “The consequences of their policies were greater, wider in scope and more momentous than the individuals themselves.”
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00495
Consider what Ibn Abi al-Hadid wrote in his Commentary on the Peak of Eloquence:
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00496

“The Prophet's own companions used to criticise one another. Had they considered themselves above criticism, they would have known it from their own circumstances. The generation that followed them took the same approach towards the companions and spoke in these terms of those who did wrong among them.”
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00497
If we are entitled to criticise the policies of the revered Rightly Guided Caliphs, are we to place the Umayyad monarchy and the Persian-style rule of the Abbasids beyond criticism?
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00498

What do Yazid ibn Muawiya, with his sinful ways, al-Walid the drunkard, Abu al-Abbas the Blood-Shedder and al-Amin the libertine have in common with Abu Bakr, who was among the first to embrace Islam, Umar with his justice, or Ali with his deep understanding of the faith? The damage done by the policies of many Umayyad and Abbasid caliphs gives us every reason to place them on the right, and their opponents, who fought for the justice Islam calls for, on the left — not to call the latter a counter-revolution. None of this amounts to the slightest attack on Islam, as Mr Salim seems to imagine.
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00499

From this misunderstanding, Mr Salim has drawn an even more mistaken conclusion. He interprets our defence of the left's right to act in secret as an attempt to “persuade modern Muslims that Islam is a revolution that depends on organised underground activity”. We said no such thing. All we said was that underground activity was a way of conducting a struggle against a formidable enemy. What has this to do with Islam itself?! This leads him into another fallacy: he denies that such a method can ever be legitimate, because, in his words, “the finest moments in the struggle of the prophets were those when they spoke out openly, with a clear and resounding call”. I would like Mr Salim to explain a fact familiar even to primary school pupils. For nearly three years, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) called people to Islam in secret, until his Lord commanded him: “Proclaim what you have been commanded to proclaim and turn away from those who worship other gods. We are enough to protect you against those who mock you.” Can Mr Salim dispute God's words: “Let believers not take unbelievers as allies in preference to believers. Whoever does so has nothing to do with God, unless you are taking precautions to protect yourselves against them”? Does this verse not justify taqiyya — concealing one's beliefs and acting in secret — when faced with a ruthless opponent?
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00500

Mr Salim has muddled his way into inventing terms of his own and attaching them to the author, whom he accuses of shu'ubiyya and materialism. He says the author follows “the modern anti-Arab interpretation of Islam, and this dubious interpretation is the very same thing as the materialist interpretation of history”! From this, I am quite certain that he understands neither what shu'ubiyya means nor what the materialist interpretation of history is about.
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00501

Shu'ubiyya is built on ethnic loyalties, ancestry and descent. It takes regionalism and nationalism as its goals. Historical materialism, on the other hand, focuses on the way society is divided into classes and takes an all-embracing, worldwide view. As a historical term, shu'ubiyya describes the response of the mawali — Muslims of non-Arab origin — to Arab dominance in the Umayyad age. It had two wings. One was moderate and included enlightened people who called for equality among all peoples in keeping with the principles of Islam. The other was extremist and insisted on ethnic distinctions. How can we possibly reconcile shu'ubiyya, founded on ethnicity, with historical materialism, founded on class? Only in Mr Salim's imagination can the two be made to fit together.
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00502

In my approach to history, I do not look for a single explanation for everything. My analysis takes a broad view, considering political, economic and social factors and the way they interact and work together to bring about historical events. There is nothing necessarily dialectical-materialist about such a view. The historian al-Masudi took this approach in his Meadows of Gold, in which he described “the circumstances of nations and the regions of the world... their beliefs and customs, the countries, mountains and seas, the kingdoms and states, and the different groups of Arab and non-Arab peoples”. Ibn Khaldun himself also referred to this approach when he developed a philosophy of history, treating it as “the study of human civilisation”. Some European scholars of Islamic history have applied this method, and they were not necessarily Marxists. Readers need only look at the work of the Italian scholar Caetani, the French scholar Massignon and the English scholar Bernard Lewis to see the truth of what I say. Mr Salim's accusations of shu'ubiyya and materialism are nothing more than an unacceptable attempt to discredit the author. His attack rebounds on him. His own article betrays that very ethnic bias when he speaks of Arab rule on Arab soil in ages when Islam — not Arab identity — was the dominant influence.
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00503

Mr Salim goes on with his false accusations. I ask him: was he being honest when he twisted the author's words and attributed statements to him that he never made? Here is an example. He says that I “with the brazen hostility of an anti-Arab partisan, accuse the community of the Prophet's city and the first home of Islam of having built its religious mission on the legacy of other civilisations, and claim that the Islamic empire owed its culture and civilisation to the Library of Alexandria, Christian monasteries and Jewish synagogues”. Readers can turn back to my exact words: “We do not deny that the Islamic left benefited from the heritage of Greek civilisation, Jewish traditions and the cultures of the East.” There is a world of difference between depending on something and benefiting from it. Elsewhere, we made the same point: “Islamic thought in general, and political thought in particular, could hardly close its eyes to the experiences of earlier societies, which already existed in the Islamic world.” Notice that we spoke of Islamic thought — philosophy and the reasoned study of religious belief — and not of the Islamic religious mission, as Mr Salim claims. He is trying to saddle us with a serious accusation by putting into our mouths the words of European scholars such as Becker, Goldziher and Grégoire, who attacked the Islamic faith with a deplorable degree of prejudice and regarded it as a distorted imitation of certain Eastern Christian sects. I would like to put an end to this attempt by informing him that we have written studies and research papers in which we discussed these views and refuted their proponents' claims with reason and evidence. Mr Salim is welcome to read them.
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00504

Mr Salim has misunderstood the term dar al-Islam, taking it to mean the Prophet's city. Dar al-Islam means the entire Islamic world, as distinct from dar al-harb (the “territory of war”), meaning non-Islamic countries. The Prophet's city (peace and blessings be upon him), on the other hand, was known as dar al-hijra, the “home of the migration”. Mr Salim should consult The Rules of Government to learn what these terms mean before he gets himself into trouble by hurling accusations without any basis.
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00505

What Mr Salim says about the Qarmatians is sheer nonsense. He claims that “the Qarmatian movement was one of the secret movements that sought to establish a settler presence in the Arab homeland... paving the way for its military conquest on behalf of a foreign power”.
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00506

I would like to correct some of his information. The Qarmatian leader was not called Hamdan ibn Qarmat, as he says, but Hamdan ibn al-Ash'ath. Qarmat was his nickname, not his father's name. Nor is the word derived from Aramaic in the sense of “deceiver”, as he claims on the authority of Father Anastas al-Karmali. An explanation based on the origin of a word carries little weight when set against explanations that arise from historical reality and fit the nature of the movement. Scholars of Islamic history follow the explanation offered by the Orientalist Ivanov, who says that qarmat means “peasant”, and that the people of southern Iraq still use it in that sense. This fits the nature of the movement, for at its heart it was a “peasant revolution”.
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00507

Mr Salim also attacks the Qarmatians, accusing them of “permitting immoral acts... and treating women as common property”. This is the same old charge, repeated over and over by the movement's enemies among the official historians. Bernard Lewis refuted it in his doctoral thesis on the origins of Ismailism, on the strength of the high standing women enjoyed in Qarmatian society. A contemporary Arab scholar, Muhammad Alyan, also refuted it in his master's thesis on The Qarmatians of Iraq. After critically examining the sources, he concluded: “We cannot support the claim that these practices were widespread. Had they been so, the ties of marriage would have weakened, but nothing of the kind is apparent in their lives. When Zakrawayh's daughter's brothers killed her husband, the stand she took against them showed just how strong the marital bond was... Moreover, the promiscuity in question would have weakened family lines among the Qarmatians, if not destroyed them completely. We have seen no evidence of this among the Qarmatians of Iraq or any other Ismaili groups.”
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00508

Mr Salim's call for us to renew our culture from its original sources is a worthy one. But such renewal cannot be accomplished in a backward-looking spirit, with a backward-looking mind. What we desperately need is a fresh reading of the old texts. Dr Hussein Mu'nis called for this when he urged us to rewrite Islamic history. Abd al-Rahman al-Sharqawi also pointed to it in his article “Blood and Truth in Islam”, in issue 2313 of Rose al-Yusuf.
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00509

Finally, I regret to say that I cannot grant Ahmad Musa Salim's request that I reconsider the ideas put forward in my article. Instead, I advise him to spend many years reading — may God grant him a long life — and then read the article again. Perhaps God will help him understand it then.
Criticising an Approach Without Having One
passage-en-00510

Here is what he wrote:
The Qarmatians Were Neither Muslims nor Socialists
passage-en-00513

It was to Dr Mahmoud Ismail's credit — despite some of his words of abuse — that, in his reply to my article, he backed away from some of the cornerstones and sacred truths of his thinking that he had championed so fervently in his earlier articles. He must have felt the weight of the connection between his promotion of the Qarmatian experiment in our own age and the charge that he subscribes to shu'ubiyya. Nor could he find a way around my assertion that the method he claims as his own is that of the Marxist Orientalist Bandali Jawzi and his school of thought. So he resorted to evasion and denial. Just to save face, he asks me in his reply: “How can anyone reconcile shu'ubiyya, founded on ethnicity, with historical materialism, founded on class, within a single approach?” The simple answer, which he knows but will not admit, is that the Orientalists who follow historical materialism have adopted all the anti-Arab claims of the secret Ismaili movements. They have taken a particular interest in the Qarmatian organisation for obvious reasons, then recast all this ethnic thinking in a new form, founded — despite a few concessions — on historical materialism. There, then, is the explanation of what the doctor could not understand: how shu'ubiyya and historical materialism came together in a single approach which he, along with many others, adopted and passed off as one of the pinnacles of scholarship!
The Qarmatians Were Neither Muslims nor Socialists
passage-en-00514

The doctor continues his cleverly disguised retreat. He denies that his way of interpreting Islamic history is based on historical materialism and tries to tell us that his all-embracing approach is the product of his own thinking. He writes:

I have followed with great interest the series of articles Dr Mahmoud Ismail began publishing on secret political movements in Islam, as well as Ahmad Musa Salim's response. Both colleagues have given me reason to put pen to paper. I believe the subject is important enough to warrant a third voice — someone to bring its wider implications into focus and point out the pitfalls along the way.

No one would deny the value of the work some of our historians are doing to rewrite particular periods of Islamic history, using modern methods and a modern style of writing. Naturally, when they examine historical events, they look at the broad changes in the economic and social life of Muslim communities as they actually lived at the time. Those communities may have remained faithful to all the principles of Islam, or departed from some of them under pressures from within or through contact with neighbouring societies.

Several of our historians have taken this approach. Taha Hussein's The Great Civil Strife and Abd al-Rahman al-Sharqawi's Muhammad, the Messenger of Freedom are examples. Al-Sharqawi also followed it to a large extent in The Struggle of the Messenger. I do not think my colleague Ahmad Musa Salim objects to this approach in principle. But his reservations undoubtedly carry weight, especially when it comes to viewing historical events in purely material terms and attributing their course and development entirely to material causes or motives. We cannot accept that as the basis for explaining the history of Muslim societies. The Islamic approach to history does not give spiritual matters priority over material ones, or material matters priority over spiritual ones. It keeps the two in proper balance.
